lesson.lesson_summary: Learners sort nouns into things we count one by one and masses we cannot count, using the count test. They meet the main groups of uncountable nouns, count a mass with unit words such as 'a bag of', and see nouns like coffee and paper that can be both. Articles and quantifiers are left to Chapter 1.4.

learning_objectives.description: Use the count test to tell countable from uncountable nouns.
success_criteria: Explain what a countable noun is.

learning_objectives.description: Recognise the main groups of uncountable nouns.
success_criteria: Name liquids, grains, gases, ideas and mass words as uncountable groups.
Recognise mass words like luggage as uncountable.

learning_objectives.description: Count an uncountable noun with a unit word.
success_criteria: Use units such as 'a glass of' and 'a bag of'.
Choose the unit word that fits a noun.

learning_objectives.description: Recognise nouns that can be countable or uncountable with different meanings.
success_criteria: Explain the difference between coffee and a coffee.

learning_dimensions.dimension: Counting a Mass With Unit Words

pages.title: Can You Count It?

content.text: You can count mangoes: one, two, three. But we never say one rice or two rices. Some nouns can be counted and some cannot.

examples.sentence: We bought six mangoes and some rice.
examples.explanation: Mangoes can be counted one by one. Rice is a mass of tiny grains, so we don't count it that way.

pages.key_takeaway: Some nouns can be counted; some cannot.

pages.title: Countable Nouns

content.text: A countable noun names something you can count one by one. It has a singular form and a plural form.

examples.sentence: Two kittens slept in the basket.
examples.explanation: We can count kittens: one kitten, two kittens.

examples.sentence: I need three pencils for the test.
examples.explanation: Pencil is countable: one pencil, three pencils.

pages.key_takeaway: Countable nouns have a singular and a plural form.

pages.title: The Count Test

content.rule_text: Put a number before the noun. If 'one ___, two ___s' sounds right, the noun is countable.
content.scope: Everyday English; a few nouns change meaning when counted (see page 9).

examples.explanation: Two bottles sounds right, so bottle is countable.

examples.sentence: The children played in the sand.
examples.explanation: Two sands sounds wrong, so sand is uncountable.

pages.key_takeaway: If a number fits before it, the noun is countable.

pages.title: Uncountable Nouns

content.text: An uncountable noun names something we think of as a mass, not as separate pieces. It has no plural form.

examples.sentence: Fresh air came through the window.
examples.explanation: We cannot count air one by one, so air is uncountable.

examples.sentence: Mum added salt to the curry.
examples.explanation: Salt is a mass of tiny grains, so it is uncountable.

pages.key_takeaway: Uncountable nouns have no plural form.

pages.title: Groups of Uncountable Nouns

content.text: Many uncountable nouns belong to one of these groups.

items: Grains and powders: rice, flour, sand

pages.key_takeaway: Liquids, powders, gases and ideas are often uncountable.

pages.title: Many Items, One Mass Word

content.text: Some words name a set of many items but are still uncountable: furniture, luggage, equipment and information.

examples.sentence: Our luggage filled the car boot.
examples.explanation: Luggage means many bags, but the word itself is uncountable.

examples.sentence: The new furniture arrived on Monday.
examples.explanation: Furniture means tables, chairs and beds together. It has no plural.

pages.key_takeaway: Some words for many items are still uncountable.

pages.title: Units Make a Mass Countable

content.text: To count an uncountable noun, put a unit word before it, such as a glass of, a bag of or a piece of. Then count the unit.

examples.sentence: Please buy two bags of flour.
examples.explanation: We count the bags, not the flour.

examples.sentence: She gave me a useful piece of advice.
examples.explanation: Advice is uncountable, so we count it in pieces.

pages.key_takeaway: Count the unit, not the mass.

pages.title: Common Unit Words

content.text: Each unit word fits certain nouns.

pages.key_takeaway: A unit word lets you count a mass noun.

pages.title: Coffee or a Coffee?

items.label: Countable
items.example: We ordered two coffees at the café.

comparison_points: Coffee as a drink in general has no plural.
A coffee means one cup, so it can be counted.
content.conclusion: Some nouns change their meaning when they are counted.

content.title: Also
content.text: Paper is the material, but a paper can mean a newspaper.

pages.key_takeaway: Counting can change what a noun means.

pages.title: Count It or Measure It

items: Countable nouns: one book, two books.
Uncountable nouns have no plural: rice, air, advice.
Use the count test: one ___, two ___s.
Unit words count a mass: a bag of flour.
Some nouns can be both: coffee and a coffee.

pages.key_takeaway: Count the things; measure the mass.

question_bank.explanation: One chair, two chairs sounds right, so chair is countable.

question_bank.prompt: Sand is countable because we can say 'two sands'.
question_bank.explanation: Two sands sounds wrong. Sand is a mass of grains, so it is uncountable.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the countable noun in: 'She poured juice into four glasses.'
question_bank.target: The noun you can count one by one.
question_bank.explanation: One glass, four glasses sounds right, so glasses is countable. Juice is a liquid, so it is uncountable.
Flour is a powder we cannot count one by one, so it is uncountable.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the uncountable noun in: 'The scientist trapped steam in a jar.'
question_bank.target: The noun that names a gas.
question_bank.explanation: Steam is a gas, so it is uncountable. Scientist and jar can be counted.

question_bank.prompt: Luggage is uncountable, even though it means many bags.
question_bank.explanation: Luggage is a mass word: it names many items together and has no plural.

question_bank.prompt: Choose the best unit word: 'I ate a ___ of bread.'
question_bank.explanation: We cut bread into slices, so 'a slice of bread' fits.

question_bank.prompt: Complete with a unit word: 'Can I have two ___ of water?'
question_bank.explanation: Water is uncountable, so we count containers of it: two glasses or two bottles of water.

question_bank.prompt: In 'Grandpa reads two papers every morning', what are the papers?
question_bank.explanation: Counted papers here are newspapers. Paper as a material is uncountable.

question_bank.prompt: In 'Coffee grows on tall bushes', coffee is uncountable.
question_bank.explanation: Here coffee means the plant and drink in general, not cups, so it is uncountable.

question_bank.prompt: Which group contains only uncountable nouns?
question_bank.explanation: Honey is a liquid, oxygen is a gas and knowledge is an idea. Cups, plates and coins can be counted.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the uncountable noun in: 'The tourists asked the guard for information.'
question_bank.target: The noun that has no plural form.
question_bank.explanation: Information is a mass word, so it is uncountable. Tourists and guard can be counted.

question_bank.prompt: Which unit word fits: 'Add a ___ of oil to the pan'?
question_bank.explanation: Oil is a liquid, so we measure it in drops.

question_bank.prompt: Chair is countable, but furniture is uncountable.
question_bank.explanation: We say one chair, two chairs. Furniture names many items as one mass, so it has no plural.

question_bank.prompt: Match each unit word with a noun it fits.
question_bank.explanation: A slice of cheese, a carton of milk and a sack of cement.
